content: These plants are native to cool temperate and arctic regions across Asia, Europe, and North America, with the greatest species diversity found in alpine habitats of the Himalayas and central Asia. Commonly referred to as saw-wort or snow lotus, the latter name is specifically applied to several high-altitude species in central Asia. These plants are perennial and herbaceous, with their height ranging from diminutive alpine species measuring 5–10 cm to taller, thistle-like plants that can grow up to 3 meters. The leaves are arranged in a dense basal rosette and spiral along the flowering stem. The flowers are grouped into dense heads of small capitula, often enveloped by dense woolly hairs that range in color from white to purple. The individual florets also exhibit similar coloration. The woolly covering is most pronounced in high-altitude species, serving to regulate flower temperature, minimize frost damage during nighttime, and protect against ultraviolet radiation from intense sunlight at high elevations. These plants are among the most difficult to grow, as they are adapted to extreme climates at altitudes of 3,500–5,000 meters. They require cool temperatures, an extended winter dormancy period lasting 8–10 months, and well-drained, humus-rich gravel soils. This species is utilized as an anti-inflammatory agent and is a component of the traditional Tibetan medicine Padma 28. This species has demonstrated anti-inflammatory, cardiotonic, abortifacient, anticancer, and antifatigue properties. However, due to overharvesting, the slow-growing wild populations of this plant are endangered. Tissue-cultured substitutes have been proposed as an alternative, offering similar therapeutic properties. Each species is adapted to its specific ecological niche, with many exhibiting unique morphological and physiological traits suited to their environments.
